args.text: The Community Garden Opens for Spring

args.alt_text: Illustration of the community garden: raised beds of lettuce, tomatoes and flowers behind a picket fence.

args.text: Opening morning: volunteers fill the new raised beds along the south fence.

Seed swap on the first Saturday of every month.
The tool shed has a new padlock: ask a steward for the code.
Rain barrels arrive on 15 April.
The hens are back: egg rota on the shed door.
New steward wanted for the herb border.

After a long, wet winter the gates of the Maple Court community garden swung open last Saturday, and forty neighbours were waiting with spades, wheelbarrows and flasks of tea. By lunchtime every one of the twelve new raised beds had been filled, levelled and raked.
The beds were built over three weekends in February by the Tuesday woodworking group, using timber donated by Harlow & Sons. Each bed has been given to a household, a school class or a local group, and the waiting list for next season already holds nineteen names.
Garden steward Maria Okafor said the early planting plan is deliberately modest. “Lettuce, radishes, peas and spinach first,” she explained. “Tomatoes and beans go in after the last frost, around the middle of May.”
New this year is a shared herb border beside the path, planted with thyme, chives, mint and sage. Everyone is welcome to pick a handful for the kitchen, and a laminated guide on the gate shows which leaves to take.
The committee also thanks the Maple Court Lions for funding the new water butts, which will collect enough rain from the shed roof to see the beds through a dry July.
The first job of the season was the compost. Over winter the three bays behind the shed were turned twice by the Thursday group, and the oldest bay is now dark, crumbly and ready to spread. Steward Tom Reyes says the trick is patience and a good mix of greens and browns. “Kitchen peelings are the greens,” he told the crowd, “and the cardboard from your parcels is the browns.”
Children were not forgotten. Class 4 from Fairview Primary School planted a bed of sunflowers, beans and pumpkins that they will visit every month until the harvest, measuring, drawing and, with luck, eating what they grow. Their teacher, Ms Patel, says it is the best classroom they have ever had, and it has no walls at all.
Several newcomers joined this year after a leaflet drive in March. Among them is Ahmed Hassan, who moved to Maple Court in January and had never grown anything before. “I came for the tea and stayed for the tomatoes,” he laughed, holding up a tray of seedlings that had already outgrown their pots.
Looking ahead, the committee has three big projects for the summer: a covered seating area beside the herb border, a path of recycled paving to the far beds so that wheelchairs and pushchairs can reach every plot, and a small orchard of apple, plum and pear trees along the north wall. Quotes for the paving are being collected now, and the committee would be glad of help with the grant application.
Plot holders are reminded that the garden rules are pinned inside the shed door. In short: be kind, close the gate, share the water, and leave your plot a little better than you found it. The next committee meeting takes place after the seed swap on the third of April, and everybody, whether or not they hold a bed, is warmly invited to come along and have their say. Tea and cake will be served, as always, and the hall is step-free with a ramp at the side door.
A garden is a conversation between neighbours that never quite ends.

Twelve new raised beds are planted and labelled
Water butts arrive on 15 April, courtesy of the Lions
The herb border is open to everyone: pick what you need
Beehive inspection on 2 May: bring a veil or borrow one
Please keep the side gate closed so the hens stay in
From Plot to Plate: Our First Harvest Supper

args.alt_text: Illustration of a wooden crate of carrots, tomatoes, beetroot, lettuce and a squash.

args.text: Last autumn's harvest, ready for the supper table.

Last October more than sixty people sat down at one long table in the Maple Court hall to eat soup, bread and roasted vegetables that had all been grown within a hundred metres of the front door.
The supper raised enough to pay for the new greenhouse glazing, and several guests asked for the recipes. We have collected them in a small booklet, free at the next seed swap.

Sign in at the garden gate and collect a name badge
Pick up a trowel and gloves from the tool shed
Choose a job from the board: weeding, watering or planting
Bring a friend and stay for tea at noon

Every bed, bench and bean pole in the garden was built or planted by a neighbour giving up a weekend. This year more than ninety people signed the volunteer book, and together they put in an estimated seven hundred hours.
If you would like to help, there is a job for every skill and every level of fitness, from watering on a summer evening to keeping the accounts.
